title: "I'm right-brained": myth or fact?
teaser: Creative people use the right side of the brain, logical people the left? A 2013 study of 1,011 brain scans looked for left- and right-brained people.

slides.alt: Cover: Myth or Fact? No. 02. 'I'm right-brained.' Creative people run on the right side of the brain, logical people on the left. Myth or fact? Make your call, then swipe. A giant marigold question mark fills the top right.
The claim: each of us has a dominant side of the brain, and it shapes how we think. 'Left-brained': logical, analytical, detail-minded. 'Right-brained': creative, intuitive, big-picture.

The test: in 2013, researchers went looking for left- and right-brained people. They mapped connections across each brain and asked whether anyone had a whole left or right network that was more strongly connected. 1,011 people aged 7 to 29, from public brain-scan data. Source: Nielsen and colleagues, 2013, PLOS ONE.
The verdict: Myth. '…our data are not consistent with a whole-brain phenotype of greater left-brained or greater right-brained network strength across individuals.' Nielsen and colleagues, 2013.

What is true: some connections lean one way; whole people don't. The scans found hubs where connections lean left (9) or right (11), but lateralisation looked like a local rather than global property of brain networks.
For teachers and designers: retire 'left-brained' and 'right-brained' labels. The scans found no such people. Send this to someone who swears they're right-brained.

body: "I'm right-brained." The idea: creative people run on the right side of the brain, logical people on the left.

In 2013, researchers analysed resting brain scans from 1,011 people aged 7 to 29, looking for anyone whose whole left or right network was more strongly connected. They didn't find them: the data were "not consistent with a whole-brain phenotype of greater 'left-brained' or greater 'right-brained' network strength across individuals."
What they did find: particular hubs where connections lean left or right. Lateralisation looked like a local property of brain networks, not a type of person. Verdict: myth.
Send this to someone who swears they're right-brained.
forDesigners: Retire 'left-brained' and 'right-brained' labels. The scans found no such people.

sources.label: Nielsen, J.A., Zielinski, B.A., Ferguson, M.A., Lainhart, J.E. & Anderson, J.S. (2013). An evaluation of the left-brain vs. right-brain hypothesis with resting state functional connectivity magnetic resonance imaging. PLOS ONE, 8(8), e71275.
